content: Asthma education is considered a critical component in the management of asthma, as outlined in national guidelines. Factors such as race, ethnicity, and socio-economic status are closely linked to markers of asthma severity, including frequent acute visits to emergency healthcare facilities. Globally, Indigenous populations are disproportionately affected by severe asthma. Developing appropriate models of care is essential for the effective delivery of healthcare services and is likely to contribute to better outcomes for individuals with asthma. The objective of this study was to evaluate whether the involvement of an Indigenous healthcare worker (IHW) in asthma education programs improves asthma-related outcomes in Indigenous children and adults with asthma, compared to programs without the involvement of an IHW. To address this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), the Cochrane Airways Group Specialised Register, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, as well as review articles and reference lists of relevant studies. The most recent search was performed in January 2011. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials that compared asthma education programs involving an IHW to those without an IHW for Indigenous individuals with asthma. Two independent reviewers selected studies for inclusion, and one reviewer extracted the data. Both reviewers independently assessed the quality of the studies. Authors of the studies were contacted for additional information when necessary. Since it was not feasible to analyze the data using an intention-to-treat approach, the data were analyzed based on treatment received. Only one study met the inclusion criteria. This study involved 113 children who were randomized to participate in an asthma education program that included an IHW, compared to a similar program without an IHW. Of these, 88 children completed the trial. The results showed that parents in the intervention group had significantly higher asthma knowledge scores (mean difference [MD] 7.49; 95% confidence interval [CI] 5.52 to 9.46) and asthma skill scores (MD 0.98; 95% CI 0.52 to 1.44) compared to the control group. Additionally, school-aged children in the intervention group had fewer days of school absence, with 100% missing fewer than 7 days, compared to 21% of the control group missing 7-14 days (difference = 21%; 95% CI 5-36%). However, there was no significant difference between the groups in the mean number of asthma exacerbations per year. Similarly, there was no significant difference in quality of life or children's asthma skill scores, although the direction of the results favored the IHW group. It is important to note that these outcomes were limited to a single study, and no studies involving adults were identified. The authors concluded that the involvement of an IHW in asthma education programs for Indigenous children with asthma was beneficial in improving most, but not all, asthma-related outcomes. While the frequency of exacerbations did not differ significantly between groups, the overall findings suggest that the inclusion of IHWs is likely to be advantageous. However, due to the limited evidence and the complexity of health outcomes and cultural factors, further randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm these findings. Despite this, the inclusion of IHWs in asthma education programs for Indigenous populations is justified, particularly given the importance of cultural self-determination and the potential for improved health outcomes.
